script.title: Sarah Hale wrote to five presidents. Only one said yes 🤯
sentences: Sarah Hale spent 17 years writing to presidents about Thanksgiving.
Back then, each state picked its own date, from October to January.
In the South, it was largely unknown.
Hale edited Godey's Lady's Book, the most widely circulated magazine of its day, and pushed it every November.
She wrote to Zachary Taylor, Millard Fillmore, Franklin Pierce and James Buchanan.
In 1863 she wrote to Abraham Lincoln.
That year he proclaimed a national Thanksgiving, joining only Washington's Birthday and Independence Day.
Not bad for the woman who also wrote Mary Had a Little Lamb.
script.description:
Thanksgiving was a patchwork of state holidays until one editor refused to give up.
The 17-year letter campaign behind the fourth Thursday.
claims_en: Sarah Josepha Hale's advocacy for a national Thanksgiving lasted 17 years.
She wrote to presidents in support of the holiday.
Each state scheduled its own Thanksgiving, some as early as October and others as late as January.
Thanksgiving was largely unknown in the American South.
Hale was editor of Godey's Lady's Book, the most widely circulated magazine before the Civil War.
Every November Hale focused her magazine column on Thanksgiving.
She wrote to Zachary Taylor, Millard Fillmore, Franklin Pierce and James Buchanan, and her initial letters failed to persuade.
Her letter to Abraham Lincoln convinced him; in 1863 Lincoln proclaimed a national day of Thanksgiving.
Before Thanksgiving, the only national holidays were Washington's Birthday and Independence Day.
Hale wrote the nursery rhyme Mary Had a Little Lamb.
scenes: Extreme close-up of Sarah Josepha Hale, a determined woman in her late 50s in a black 1850s mourning dress with dark ringlet curls, quill in hand, eyes burning with resolve, candlelight.
An 1840s American map on a wooden table with autumn harvest tables scattered across different seasons, Hale studying it with a frown, warm lamplight, medium shot, no readable text.
A quiet 1840s Southern town square in autumn with no celebration, empty streets, soft grey light, wide shot.
Hale at a busy 1850s Philadelphia editor's desk piled with magazine proofs, writing intently, a November window with falling leaves behind her, medium shot, no readable text.
Hale sealing a stack of letters with red wax, each addressed envelope piling up, focused tired face, candlelit study, close shot, no readable text.
Hale reading a short polite reply letter, lips pressed together, setting it on a pile of other replies, dim evening light, medium close-up, no readable text.
Hale, older now, writing one more letter with a steady hand beside a candle and a tall stack of earlier letters, lamplight, medium shot, no readable text.
A family gathered around a roast turkey dinner in an 1860s American home, warm candlelight, Hale smiling quietly at the head of the table, wide shot.
Hale with a small wry smile beside a little girl and a white lamb in a New England schoolyard, golden afternoon light, medium shot.
